title: India Is About to Flood the Market With $6 Billion in New Shares. Here Is What Every NRI Investor Needs to Know.
excerpt: Zepto just filed for $837 million. NSE is close behind at $2.5 billion. Jio looms. And 163 companies already have SEBI approval. The second half of 2026 could reshape India's equity market.
body:
The first half of 2026 was quiet. Indian IPOs raised about $3.5 billion through June, according to Bloomberg data, well behind the $20 billion pace of each of the two previous record-breaking years.

The second half will not be quiet.

A Bloomberg analysis published this week estimates that Indian companies are set to raise approximately Rs 60,000 crore — roughly $6 billion — through IPOs, institutional placements, and government stake sales in the coming months. Add lock-in expiry releases, and the total share supply entering the market could be staggering.

For NRI investors, this is the most consequential pipeline India has seen in years. And it demands attention.

The Three IPOs That Will Define the Year

Zepto filed updated draft papers on June 8 for an IPO that could raise $837 million, making it one of the year's most anticipated listings. The quick-commerce company, which delivers groceries in 10 minutes across Indian metros, more than doubled its revenue to Rs 226 billion ($2.36 billion) in the year ending March 2026. Losses widened to Rs 59 billion, but in India's growth-obsessed market, that has not deterred investor appetite.

Zepto is targeting a July listing. Axis Capital, Morgan Stanley, Goldman Sachs, Motilal Oswal, HSBC, JM Financial, and IIFL Capital are managing the offering. Existing investors including Nexus Ventures and Contrary ZEP Holdings will sell up to 113.5 million shares.

The National Stock Exchange of India (NSE) — the bourse that runs the market — may follow with a filing valued at approximately $2.5 billion. An NSE listing would be a landmark moment for Indian capital markets, giving investors direct exposure to the infrastructure of India's equity boom.

And looming over all of it is Reliance Jio Platforms, which could raise upwards of $4 billion in what would be India's largest-ever IPO. A 2.5 per cent stake sale alone could generate roughly Rs 37,500 crore. The timeline remains uncertain, with market watchers pointing to the second half of FY27, but when it arrives, it will instantly become a top-three Indian company by market cap.

The Supply Wall

Beyond the marquee names, the pipeline is vast. According to data from Prime Database, 163 companies have already received approval from the Securities and Exchange Board of India (SEBI) to launch IPOs. Another 62 have filed draft prospectuses and are awaiting regulatory clearance. India is, by this measure, one of the world's most active primary markets.

And then there are the lock-in expiries. According to Nuvama Wealth Management, lock-up periods will expire for more than 75 listed companies over the next four months, potentially freeing up to $31 billion worth of stocks. Not all of these shares will hit the market — promoter holdings account for a significant portion — but the supply overhang is real.

"This sustained pace of issuance indicates healthy underlying liquidity and participation across domestic institutions, foreign investors and retail segments," said Samarth Jagnani, head of global capital markets for India and Southeast Asia at Morgan Stanley.

Some investors are less sanguine. If multiple large offerings launch simultaneously, the market's absorptive capacity will be tested.

What NRIs Need to Know

For diaspora investors, the opportunity comes with regulatory guardrails. FEMA (Foreign Exchange Management Act) rules govern NRI participation in Indian IPOs. The key considerations:

PIS account required. NRIs investing in Indian equities need a Portfolio Investment Scheme (PIS) account linked to an NRE or NRO bank account. Many banks offer this through their NRI divisions, but setup can take weeks — so start now if you have not already.

Sectoral caps apply. Foreign investment limits vary by sector. Quick commerce (Zepto) falls under e-commerce, where 100 per cent FDI is permitted under the automatic route. Financial infrastructure (NSE) may carry stricter limits.

Tax implications are real. Short-term capital gains on listed equities are taxed at 20 per cent for NRIs. Long-term gains above Rs 1.25 lakh attract 12.5 per cent tax. DTAA benefits may apply depending on the NRI's country of residence, but claiming them requires proper documentation including a Tax Residency Certificate.

Timing matters. The IPO application window is typically three to five days. NRIs should ensure their demat and PIS accounts are active and funded well before a listing they want to participate in.

The Bigger Picture

India's primary market is evolving from a periodic event into a continuous pipeline. The breadth of sectors represented — quick commerce, financial infrastructure, telecom, insurance, consumer brands — reflects an economy that is deepening its capital markets in real time.

The risk is dilution. When too many companies compete for the same pool of institutional and retail capital, pricing discipline can erode. The first half's sluggishness was partly driven by tariff fears and oil price volatility from the Middle East crisis, and those headwinds have not disappeared.

But for NRIs with long-term India exposure in mind, the second half of 2026 offers a menu of entry points that did not exist a year ago. The question is not whether to pay attention. It is whether your accounts are ready.
